questions.question: Which nutrient provides a significant amount of energy during lower- / intensity, long-duration exercise? a). Fat b). Protein c). Vitamin C d). Calcium
questions.solution_html:
• Which nutrient provides a significant amount of energy during lower-intensity, long-duration
  • exercise?
  • Answer: A. Fat
  • Answer: A. Reduces the use of amino acids for energy
  • During-exercise hydration
  • • Athletes should drink fluids at regular intervals according to thirst, sweat rate, exercise
  • intensity and environmental conditions.
  • • The aim is to replace fluid losses and minimize excessive dehydration during prolonged
  • exercise.
  • • Sports drinks containing carbohydrates and electrolytes are useful during endurance activities
  • lasting more than one hour because they provide energy and replace sodium losses.
  • • Athletes should develop an individualized hydration plan based on sweat rate, body weight
  • changes and previous training experience.
  • • Excessive drinking should be avoided because it can cause exercise-associated hyponatremia, a
  • dangerous decrease in blood sodium concentration.
  • • Hydration strategies should be practised during training before being used in competition.
  • Energy Density
  • • Energy density refers to the number of calories present per unit weight of food.
  • • Low-energy-density foods, such as vegetables, fruits and soups, provide fewer calories relative
  • to their weight and help promote fullness.
  • • High-energy-density foods, such as fried foods, sweets and foods rich in added fats, provide
  • more calories in smaller portions.
  • • Choosing nutrient-dense foods helps athletes meet their vitamin, mineral and fibre requirements
  • while controlling calorie intake.
  • • Appropriate portion sizes and healthy food choices support effective weight management.
  • Growth and Development
  • • Proteins are essential for the growth and development of muscles and other body tissues.
  • • Calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D support the development of strong bones and teeth.
  • • Carbohydrates and fats provide energy required for growth, physical activity and normal body
  • functions.
  • • Vitamins and minerals support brain development, hormonal functions and proper maturation.
  • • Adequate nutrition is especially important during childhood, adolescence and pregnancy.

  • Dos
  • • Drink fluids regularly according to thirst, sweat rate and environmental conditions.
  • • Use carbohydrate-containing sports drinks or foods during prolonged endurance exercise when
  • appropriate.
  • • Replace electrolytes, particularly sodium, during prolonged exercise with substantial sweat
  • losses.
  • • Follow an individualized hydration and fueling plan practised during training.
  • • Monitor fatigue, thirst and other signs of dehydration.

questions.question: When evaluating different psychological strategies for athlete weight / management, which should be prioritized as most sustainable long- term? a). Strategies focused solely on rapid appearance changes b). Strategies with no long-term follow-up c). Strategies that build resilience and healthy coping skills rather than quick-fix or appearance-focused approaches d). Strategies that avoid any professional involvement
questions.solution_html:
• When evaluating different psychological strategies for athlete weight management, which
  • should be prioritized as most sustainable long-term?
  • Answer: C. Strategies that build resilience and healthy coping skills rather than quick-fix or
  • appearance-focused approaches
  • Post-exercise hydration
  • • Athletes should replace the fluids lost through sweating to restore normal hydration levels.
  • • Body weight before and after exercise can help estimate fluid loss; each kilogram of body
  • weight lost represents approximately one litre of net fluid loss.
  • • Athletes may consume approximately 1.25–1.5 litres of fluid for every kilogram of body
  • weight lost when rapid and complete rehydration is required.
  • • Sodium-containing fluids or meals help retain consumed fluid and replace sodium lost through
  • sweat.
  • • Carbohydrate-containing drinks and foods help replenish glycogen stores, while protein
  • supports muscle repair and recovery.
  • • Athletes should continue drinking fluids with meals until hydration is restored, while avoiding
  • forced or excessive fluid consumption.
  • Proper pre-exercise, during-exercise and post-exercise hydration helps endurance athletes maintain
  • performance, regulate body temperature, prevent dehydration and support effective recovery.
  • Hydration plans should be individualized according to sweat rate, exercise duration, environmental
  • conditions and the athlete’s needs.
  • Macronutrient Distribution
  • • Carbohydrates: Provide energy for training and replenish muscle glycogen stores. Intake should
  • be adjusted according to training intensity and duration.
  • • Proteins: Support muscle repair, growth and maintenance. Adequate protein intake is
  • particularly important during a caloric deficit to reduce muscle loss.
  • • Fats: Provide essential fatty acids, support hormone production and facilitate the absorption of
  • fat-soluble vitamins.
  • • Athletes should distribute macronutrients according to their sport, training demands, body
  • composition goals and total energy requirements.
  • • A balanced diet containing adequate carbohydrates, proteins and healthy fats helps maintain
  • performance and overall health.
  • Tissue Maintenance and Repair
  • Post-exercise Phase
  • Dos
  • • Consume carbohydrates to replenish muscle glycogen stores, especially after prolonged or
  • intense exercise.
  • • Include protein to support muscle repair and recovery.
  • • Replace fluid losses using water and, when necessary, sodium-containing drinks or foods.
  • • Eat a balanced recovery meal containing carbohydrates, protein, vitamins and minerals.
  • • Begin recovery nutrition promptly when another training session or competition is scheduled
  • soon.
questions.final_answer: Option (c) Strategies that build resilience and healthy coping skills rather than quick-fix or

questions.question: What is the leucine threshold?
questions.solution_html:
• The leucine threshold is the amount of leucine, an essential branched-chain amino acid (BCAA)
  • needed in a meal to sufficiently stimulate muscle protein synthesis. It is generally around 2–3 grams
  • per meal in healthy adults, supporting muscle growth and repair.
questions.final_answer: per meal in healthy adults, supporting muscle growth and repair

questions.question: Why can dehydration before competition impair performance?
questions.solution_html:
• Dehydration before competition can reduce blood volume, increase body temperature, and cause early
  • fatigue. It can also decrease endurance, muscle strength, concentration, and coordination, leading to
  • reduced sports performance.
questions.final_answer: reduced sports performance
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the hydration plan recommended alongside pre-exercise meals
questions.solution_html:
• The hydration plan alongside pre-exercise meals involve drinking approximately 5–7 mL of water per
  • kilogram of body weight about 4 hours before exercise to ensure adequate hydration. If urine remains
  • dark or urination is insufficient, an additional 3–5 mL/kg about 2 hours before exercise may be
  • consumed. This helps maintain fluid balance, regulate body temperature, prevent dehydration, and
  • improve sports performance.
questions.final_answer: improve sports performance
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
